items.name: Model Development Lifecycle
items.summary: Every predictive or analytical model follows a documented lifecycle spanning problem definition, data preparation, modeling, validation, deployment, and ongoing monitoring. This end-to-end discipline ensures models used in pricing, underwriting, claims, and fraud detection are traceable from business question to production behavior and can withstand model risk and regulatory scrutiny.

items.name: Model Monitoring
items.summary: Governs the ongoing surveillance of production models so that degradation is detected and corrected before it affects pricing, underwriting, or claims decisions. The standard ensures every deployed model has a defined monitoring regime and a clear path back to retraining.

subs.title: Drift Detection
subs.description: Production models must be instrumented to detect statistical drift in both input features and output score distributions relative to the training baseline. Detection thresholds are set per model at deployment, and alerts route to the owning data science team so shifts in policyholder mix, claims patterns, or market conditions are caught early.

subs.title: Performance Metrics Tracked
subs.description: Each model's agreed performance measures, such as accuracy, lift, calibration, or loss-ratio impact, are computed on a defined cadence and recorded in the model inventory. Results are reviewed against the benchmarks established at validation, with trends visible to model owners and the model risk function.

subs.title: Retraining Triggers Defined
subs.description: Every production model carries documented criteria that mandate retraining or recalibration, including performance falling below threshold, sustained drift, or material business changes such as new product launches or regulatory rate filings. Triggered retraining follows the full development lifecycle rather than ad hoc refits.

items.name: Model Validation
items.summary: Establishes the independent checks a model must pass before deployment and at periodic review, covering statistical soundness, fairness, and interpretability. It protects the carrier from deploying models that are overfit, discriminatory, or unexplainable to regulators and business stakeholders.

subs.title: Holdout Validation
subs.description: Model performance must be demonstrated on a holdout dataset that was excluded from training and tuning, with results compared against the development sample to detect overfitting. The holdout design, including any time-based splits appropriate for policy and claims data, is documented in the validation report.

subs.title: Bias Testing
subs.description: Models that influence underwriting, pricing, or claims outcomes are tested for disparate impact across protected classes and proxy variables before approval. Testing methodology and results are retained as evidence for state insurance regulators, and identified disparities must be remediated or formally risk-accepted before deployment.

subs.title: Explainability Requirements
subs.description: Each model must meet an explainability bar appropriate to its use: adverse-action and rating models require reason codes or feature attributions that can be communicated to policyholders and regulators. Black-box techniques are permissible only where a documented interpretability method accompanies them.

subs.title: Model Risk Review
subs.description: Before production release, every model receives an independent review under the enterprise model risk framework, covering conceptual soundness, data lineage, assumptions, and limitations. The review assigns a risk tier that dictates the depth of ongoing monitoring and the revalidation cycle.

items.name: Dashboard Standards
items.summary: Defines the design and performance bar that all enterprise dashboards must meet so executives, underwriters, and claims leaders get a consistent, fast, and navigable analytics experience. Adherence keeps the BI estate coherent as content scales across business lines.

subs.title: Consistent Design Language
subs.description: Dashboards follow the enterprise BI style guide, including the approved color palette, typography, KPI tile layouts, and standard chart types for measures like loss ratio, premium, and claims frequency. Visual conventions carry the same meaning everywhere, so a red indicator on a P&C dashboard reads the same as on a Life & Retirement one.

subs.title: Mobile-Friendly
subs.description: Dashboards must render usably on tablets and phones, with responsive layouts or purpose-built mobile views for content consumed by field staff, agents, and traveling executives. Touch targets, legibility, and load behavior on mobile networks are verified before publication.

subs.title: Performance Under 5 Second Load
subs.description: Initial dashboard render must complete within five seconds under typical user load, validated during UAT and re-checked after material data model changes. Developers achieve this through aggregation tables, query tuning, and caching rather than by trimming required content.

subs.title: Drill-Down Capability
subs.description: Summary views must let users navigate from enterprise or line-of-business aggregates down to the underlying detail, such as moving from book-level loss ratio to region, product, and individual claim. Drill paths are designed deliberately and preserve filter context at each level.

items.name: Report Development Standards
items.summary: Governs how new reports move from request to production, ensuring each one is built against documented needs, verified for correctness, and operated on a known schedule. This keeps regulatory, financial, and operational reporting trustworthy across the carrier.

subs.title: Requirements Documented
subs.description: Every report begins with written requirements capturing the business question, intended audience, source data, calculations, and any regulatory context such as statutory or NAIC reporting obligations. Requirements are approved by the requesting business owner before development starts.

subs.title: Data Validation
subs.description: Report figures are reconciled against source systems and, where applicable, against established financial or actuarial controls before release. Validation evidence, including tie-outs of premium, reserve, and claims totals, is retained with the report's documentation.

subs.title: UAT Sign-Off
subs.description: The business owner must formally accept the report in user acceptance testing, confirming figures, filters, and layout against the documented requirements. Sign-off is recorded, and no report enters production distribution without it.

subs.title: Refresh Schedule Defined
subs.description: Each production report declares its refresh cadence, data-as-of timing, and dependencies on upstream pipeline completion. The schedule is published to consumers so users of month-end financial or daily claims reports know exactly how current the data is.

items.name: Self-Service Guidelines
items.summary: Sets the guardrails under which business users build their own analyses, balancing analytical agility with the control an insurer needs over figures that may inform filings and decisions. It ensures self-service grows on trusted, governed foundations rather than shadow data.

subs.title: Certified Datasets for Self-Service
subs.description: Self-service analysis is performed against datasets that the Data & Analytics team has certified for accuracy, definitions, and refresh reliability. Certification status is visible in the BI tools, and certified content covering policy, claims, billing, and distribution data is the default starting point for business analysts.

subs.title: Training Required
subs.description: Users must complete the prescribed enablement curriculum, covering tool usage, data interpretation, and handling of confidential policyholder data, before receiving self-service authoring rights. Access is provisioned only after training completion is recorded.

subs.title: Governed Data Sources Only
subs.description: Self-service content may connect only to approved, governed sources such as the certified semantic layer and warehouse schemas. Direct connections to operational systems, personal extracts, and unmanaged spreadsheets are prohibited as report sources, preventing shadow reporting of premium or loss figures.

items.name: Data Catalog Standards
items.summary: Requires that the enterprise data catalog serve as the complete, navigable inventory of the carrier's data assets. Full registration and enrichment make data discoverable and trustworthy for analysts, actuaries, and auditors alike.

subs.title: All Datasets Registered
subs.description: Every dataset in the warehouse, lake, and approved analytical stores must be registered in the enterprise catalog, including its description, owner, and source. New datasets are registered as part of the deployment process, so nothing reaches production undocumented.

subs.title: Business Glossary Terms Linked
subs.description: Catalog entries are linked to approved business glossary terms, such as earned premium, incurred loss, or surrender rate, so technical fields map to a single agreed business meaning. Glossary stewardship resolves conflicting definitions across P&C, Life & Retirement, and group benefits usage.

subs.title: Lineage Captured
subs.description: End-to-end lineage from source systems through transformation pipelines to reports is recorded in the catalog, automatically where tooling allows. Lineage supports impact analysis for changes and gives auditors and regulators a defensible trace of how reported figures are produced.

subs.title: Searchable
subs.description: The catalog must support search across names, descriptions, glossary terms, and tags so users can locate relevant data without insider knowledge. Search quality is maintained through metadata completeness checks and periodic curation of stale or duplicate entries.

items.name: Metadata Standards
items.summary: Defines the minimum metadata that must accompany every data asset so its meaning, stewardship, and handling requirements are never ambiguous. Complete metadata underpins catalog quality, access control, and regulatory accountability.

subs.title: Technical and Business Metadata Required
subs.description: Each asset carries both technical metadata, such as schema, data types, source system, and load mechanics, and business metadata, such as plain-language descriptions and glossary linkage. Both layers are mandatory at registration; an asset with only one is considered incomplete.

subs.title: Ownership, Classification, and Refresh Frequency Documented
subs.description: Every dataset's metadata must record its accountable owner, its sensitivity classification under the enterprise scheme, and how often it is refreshed. These three attributes drive access decisions, privacy handling for policyholder data, and consumer expectations about currency, and they are verified during periodic catalog reviews.

items.name: Data Lake Standards
items.summary: Prescribes the architecture and storage conventions for the enterprise data lake so that data from policy administration, claims, billing, and external feeds lands in a predictable, performant, and cost-efficient structure. Consistency here keeps downstream engineering and analytics interoperable.

subs.title: Medallion Architecture (Bronze/Silver/Gold)
subs.description: Lake content is organized into Bronze raw ingestion, Silver cleansed and conformed, and Gold business-ready layers, with defined promotion criteria between each. Consumers other than engineering teams work from Silver or Gold; raw Bronze data is never exposed directly to reporting or self-service.

subs.title: Partitioning Strategy
subs.description: Each dataset declares a partitioning scheme appropriate to its access patterns, typically by ingestion or business date and, where useful, by line of business or source system. Partition design is reviewed at onboarding to prevent small-file proliferation and full-table scans on large policy and claims histories.

subs.title: File Formats (Parquet/Delta)
subs.description: Persisted lake data uses Parquet, with Delta Lake required where ACID updates, merges, or time travel are needed, such as for CDC targets and Silver conformed tables. Other formats are permitted only transiently in Bronze landing zones for source fidelity.

items.name: ETL/ELT Standards
items.summary: Sets the default patterns for moving and transforming data into the analytics platform, favoring approaches that scale with the carrier's data volumes and keep every load auditable. Following these patterns keeps integration work consistent across teams and source systems.

subs.title: ELT Preferred
subs.description: Pipelines should land data in the platform first and transform it there, exploiting the warehouse and lake engines rather than external transformation servers. Traditional ETL is used only where justified, such as source-side filtering of sensitive policyholder attributes, and the exception is documented.

subs.title: Incremental Loads
subs.description: Recurring loads must process only new or changed records, using watermarks, change tracking, or comparable mechanisms, rather than full reloads of policy and claims history. Full refreshes are reserved for initial loads and documented recovery scenarios.

subs.title: Change Data Capture for Real-Time
subs.description: Where near-real-time data is required, such as claims status feeds or fraud-screening inputs, pipelines use change data capture from source databases rather than high-frequency batch polling. CDC implementations must handle deletes and schema changes and are monitored for replication lag.

subs.title: Audit Columns in All Tables
subs.description: Every managed table carries standard audit columns recording load timestamp, source identifier, and pipeline or batch ID, populated automatically by the ingestion framework. These columns make any record's provenance traceable, supporting reconciliation, regulatory inquiries, and incident investigation.

items.name: Pipeline Standards
items.summary: Defines the engineering qualities every production data pipeline must exhibit so the platform stays reliable as sources, schemas, and volumes evolve. Pipelines meeting this standard fail safely, recover cleanly, and surface problems before consumers notice them.

subs.title: Idempotent
subs.description: Pipelines must produce the same result when rerun for the same period or batch, using merge logic, deterministic keys, or overwrite-by-partition patterns. This allows operators to safely replay failed loads of premium, claims, or billing data without creating duplicates.

subs.title: Schema Evolution Handled
subs.description: Pipelines must tolerate additive source schema changes, such as new columns from a policy administration upgrade, without failing, and must fail loudly with clear diagnostics on breaking changes. The handling approach for each feed is documented alongside its data contract.

subs.title: Data Contracts Enforced
subs.description: Each pipeline validates inbound data against an agreed contract covering schema, types, nullability, and key constraints, negotiated with the producing system team. Contract violations quarantine the offending records or halt the load per the feed's criticality, rather than silently propagating bad data downstream.

subs.title: Monitoring and Alerting
subs.description: Production pipelines emit run status, duration, row counts, and data freshness metrics to the central monitoring platform, with alerts routed to the on-call engineer on failure or SLA breach. Alert thresholds reflect downstream commitments, such as month-end close and regulatory reporting deadlines.

items.name: Data Governance Framework
items.summary: Establishes the organizational machinery through which the carrier governs its data, defining who decides, how decisions are made, and how disputes get resolved. A functioning framework keeps data accountability operating continuously rather than as a one-time documentation exercise.

subs.title: Roles, Responsibilities, and Policies Documented
subs.description: The framework document defines each governance role, including data owners, stewards, custodians, and the chief data officer, with explicit responsibilities, and indexes the full set of enterprise data policies. The document is version-controlled and reviewed when organizational or regulatory changes occur.

subs.title: Data Council Meets Monthly
subs.description: A cross-functional Data Council, with representation from P&C, Life & Retirement, group benefits, IT, compliance, and actuarial, convenes monthly to approve policies, prioritize data initiatives, and adjudicate cross-domain issues. Minutes and decisions are recorded and published to stakeholders.

subs.title: Escalation Path Defined
subs.description: A documented escalation route carries unresolved data disputes from stewards to domain owners to the Data Council, with defined response timeframes at each tier. Issues with regulatory or financial-reporting exposure may be fast-tracked directly to the Council chair.

items.name: Data Ownership
items.summary: Ensures that no dataset in the enterprise is unaccountable by binding each one to named individuals responsible for its quality, access, and definition. Clear ownership is the precondition for every other governance control functioning.

subs.title: Every Dataset Has Assigned Owner and Steward
subs.description: Each registered dataset names a business data owner accountable for its content and access decisions, and a data steward responsible for day-to-day quality and definition upkeep. Ownership is assigned at dataset onboarding and recorded in the catalog; unowned datasets are flagged for remediation or retirement.

subs.title: Accountability Documented
subs.description: The specific duties of each owner and steward, including access approval, quality remediation, classification, and glossary maintenance, are written into role charters acknowledged by the assignees. Documentation makes accountability auditable when regulators or internal audit examine data handling for policyholder information.

subs.title: Annual Review
subs.description: Ownership assignments are reconfirmed at least annually, with reassignments triggered immediately by departures or reorganizations rather than waiting for the cycle. The review also verifies that owners have actively discharged their duties, such as completing access recertifications, during the period.

items.name: Data Policies
items.summary: Requires a complete, formally approved, and well-socialized body of enterprise data policy so that handling rules are consistent across business lines and defensible to regulators. The standard covers both the content of the policy set and how it gains authority and reach.

subs.title: Policies for Access, Retention, Quality, and Privacy
subs.description: The enterprise maintains current written policies covering data access control, retention and disposal, quality management, and privacy protection, addressing obligations such as state insurance data security laws and privacy statutes. Each policy names its owner and review cycle, and gaps identified by audit or regulation drive prompt updates.

subs.title: Approved by Data Council
subs.description: New policies and material revisions take effect only after formal Data Council approval, recorded in Council minutes. This single approval authority prevents divergent line-of-business rules for the same data handling question.

subs.title: Communicated Organization-Wide
subs.description: Approved policies are published in the central policy repository and communicated to all affected staff through announcements and role-appropriate training. Policies carrying compliance obligations, such as PII handling, require tracked acknowledgment from employees with access to the relevant data.

items.name: Master Data Standards
items.summary: Governs how the carrier constructs and maintains authoritative master records for core entities such as customers, producers, and providers across P&C, Life & Retirement, and group benefits systems. Disciplined mastering gives the enterprise one trusted view of each party it does business with.

subs.title: Golden Record Rules Defined
subs.description: For each mastered domain, documented rules specify which attributes constitute the golden record and which sources are authoritative for each, such as the policy administration system for coverage data and CRM for contact preferences. Rules are owned by the domain's data steward and versioned as sources change.

subs.title: Match and Merge Logic Documented
subs.description: The deterministic and probabilistic matching criteria used to identify the same customer, household, or producer across systems, along with merge thresholds and manual review bands, are fully documented and tuned against measured false-match rates. Changes to matching logic require steward approval and regression testing, since over-merging policyholder records carries privacy and servicing risk.

subs.title: Survivorship Rules
subs.description: When merged records conflict, documented survivorship rules determine which value wins per attribute, based on source trust ranking, recency, and completeness. The rules are implemented in the MDM hub rather than applied ad hoc, and overridden values remain traceable to their originating source.

items.name: Reference Data Management
items.summary: Establishes central control over the code tables and lookup values, such as state codes, line-of-business codes, and cause-of-loss codes, that every system and report depends on. Central management eliminates the silent inconsistencies that arise when each application maintains its own copies.

subs.title: Code Tables Centrally Managed
subs.description: All shared reference data is mastered in the central reference data repository, which is the sole authoritative source from which consuming systems subscribe or replicate. Industry code sets, such as NAIC and ISO classifications, are loaded and maintained centrally rather than keyed independently by each team.

subs.title: Versioned
subs.description: Reference datasets carry version identifiers and effective dates, and historical versions remain retrievable so that past reports and rate calculations can be reproduced against the codes in force at the time. Consumers can pin to a version or track the current one explicitly.

subs.title: Change Control Process
subs.description: Additions, modifications, and retirements of reference values follow a documented request and approval workflow involving the affected data stewards, with changes communicated to consuming system owners ahead of release. Emergency changes are permitted with retroactive approval and documentation.

subs.title: No Local Overrides
subs.description: Consuming applications and reports may not redefine, extend, or remap centrally managed codes locally. Where a system needs an additional value, the request goes through central change control, so a cause-of-loss or product code means the same thing in every claims report and regulatory filing.

items.name: Data Classification
items.summary: Requires that every data asset carry a sensitivity classification that drives how it is stored, shared, and protected. Reliable classification is the foundation for proportionate controls over everything from public rate filings to restricted policyholder health information.

subs.title: All Data Classified (Public/Internal/Confidential/Restricted)
subs.description: Every dataset, report, and extract is assigned one of the four enterprise sensitivity tiers at creation or onboarding, with classification criteria defined in the data classification policy. Policyholder PII, claims medical details, and underwriting files default to Confidential or Restricted, and unclassified data is treated as Confidential until assessed.

subs.title: Labeling Enforced
subs.description: Classification labels are applied through catalog metadata and, where tooling supports it, embedded sensitivity labels on files and reports, and downstream controls such as access policies, masking, and DLP rules key off those labels. Periodic scans verify that labels exist and match the actual content, with mismatches routed to data stewards for correction.

items.name: Data Retention
items.summary: Governs how long the carrier keeps each category of data and how disposal actually happens, balancing state insurance record-keeping requirements against privacy obligations to minimize held data. The standard makes retention an operational process rather than a policy statement.

subs.title: Retention Schedules by Data Type
subs.description: A maintained retention schedule assigns keep periods to each data category, reflecting state insurance record-retention regulations, statutes of limitation for claims, and contractual obligations across P&C, life, and group benefits products. The schedule is owned jointly with Legal and Compliance and reviewed when regulations change.

subs.title: Automated Purge Where Possible
subs.description: Systems and data stores implement automated deletion or archival jobs aligned to the retention schedule, with execution logs retained as evidence of disposal. Where automation is infeasible, a documented manual purge procedure with attestation applies, and the gap is tracked for remediation.

subs.title: Legal Hold Process
subs.description: A defined process suspends purge for data subject to litigation, regulatory examination, or claims disputes, with holds recorded centrally and propagated to every system housing the affected records. Holds are released only on instruction from Legal, after which normal retention resumes.

items.name: PII Handling
items.summary: Sets the mandatory safeguards for personally identifiable information across its lifecycle in the data platform, from knowing where it lives to controlling and recording every access. These controls protect policyholders and keep the carrier compliant with insurance data security and privacy laws.

subs.title: PII Inventory Maintained
subs.description: A current inventory records every dataset and system containing PII, the specific elements held, such as SSN, date of birth, health information, and financial details, and the lawful purpose for holding them. The inventory is updated as part of dataset onboarding and feeds privacy impact assessments and breach-response scoping.

subs.title: Encryption and Masking Applied
subs.description: PII is encrypted at rest and in transit, and direct identifiers are masked, tokenized, or pseudonymized in non-production environments and in analytical datasets where the identifier is not required. Masking standards specify approved techniques per element, so SSNs and bank details never appear in clear text outside controlled production use.

subs.title: Access Logged
subs.description: All access to PII-bearing datasets is logged with user identity, timestamp, and data accessed, and logs are retained per the audit policy and protected from tampering. Access patterns are reviewed for anomalies, supporting both insider-threat detection and the evidence requirements of privacy regulators.

subs.title: Retention Enforced
subs.description: PII is held no longer than the retention schedule permits, with purge and anonymization applied to identifiers even where aggregate records are kept longer for actuarial analysis. Compliance is verified through periodic sampling of PII stores against the schedule.

items.name: Data Issue Management
items.summary: Defines the disciplined process for handling data defects from discovery through permanent fix, so quality problems are resolved at their source instead of being patched repeatedly downstream. Consistent issue management turns individual incidents into systemic improvement.

subs.title: Issues Logged in Tracking System
subs.description: Every identified data issue, whether found by automated quality checks, report consumers, or auditors, is recorded in the enterprise tracking system with severity, affected datasets, business impact, and an assigned owner. Verbal or email-only reporting does not count as logged, and issue aging is reviewed by data stewards.

subs.title: Root Cause Analysis
subs.description: Issues above the defined severity threshold receive a documented root cause analysis tracing the defect to its origin, such as a source system entry gap, pipeline transformation error, or broken business process. The analysis distinguishes the immediate correction of affected records from the underlying cause.

subs.title: Prevention Measures Implemented
subs.description: Each completed root cause analysis produces preventive actions, such as new validation rules, data contract changes, or source-system fixes, with owners and due dates tracked to closure. Recurrence of a previously analyzed issue triggers escalation to the responsible domain owner.

items.name: Data Quality Rules
items.summary: Requires each data domain to define and continuously execute the quality checks appropriate to its data, and to make the results visible to the people who depend on it. Published, rule-based quality measurement replaces anecdote with evidence about whether data is fit for use.

subs.title: Data Quality Rules Defined by Data Domain
subs.description: Stewards for each domain, such as policy, claims, billing, customer, and producer data, define the completeness, validity, consistency, and uniqueness rules that matter for their data, including insurance-specific checks like valid coverage effective dates and reconciled premium amounts. Rules are documented in the quality tool with business rationale and thresholds.

subs.title: Automated Profiling
subs.description: Quality rules execute automatically on a defined cadence through the data quality platform, profiling datasets as they are loaded rather than relying on manual spot checks. New datasets are baseline-profiled at onboarding to set expectations before rules are formalized.

subs.title: Data Quality Scores Published
subs.description: Rule results roll up into quality scores per dataset and domain, published on dashboards visible to data owners, stewards, and consumers, including surfacing scores in the data catalog. Trends are reviewed in governance forums, and persistently low scores trigger remediation plans.

items.name: Data Quality SLAs
items.summary: Commits the department to quantified quality and responsiveness targets for the data it serves, giving business consumers an enforceable expectation rather than best effort. Measured SLAs anchor quality conversations between Data & Analytics and the lines of business.

subs.title: Completeness Above 99%
subs.description: Critical data elements in governed datasets must be populated for more than 99 percent of records, measured by automated completeness rules against each dataset's defined critical fields. Datasets falling below the threshold are flagged on quality dashboards and enter remediation.

subs.title: Accuracy Above 99%
subs.description: More than 99 percent of records must pass accuracy checks, validated through reconciliation to authoritative sources and conformance rules, such as premium amounts tying to the billing system and policy statuses matching administration systems. Accuracy is sampled and certified for datasets feeding financial and regulatory reporting.

subs.title: Timeliness Per Business SLA
subs.description: Each governed dataset carries an agreed availability deadline, such as daily claims data by 7 a.m. or month-end financial data within the close calendar, negotiated with its business consumers. Pipeline monitoring measures actual delivery against these commitments and reports breaches.

subs.title: Remediation Within 24 Hours
subs.description: When a dataset breaches its completeness, accuracy, or timeliness target, remediation must begin and the issue be resolved or formally triaged with a communicated plan within 24 hours. Consumers of the affected data are notified promptly so downstream decisions and reports are not made on known-bad data.
